hormone.short: A chemical messenger released by a gland into the blood. It reaches every tissue but acts only on cells that carry a receptor for it.

receptor.short: A protein, on the cell surface or inside the cell, that binds one hormone (or transmitter) and sets off the cell's response. No receptor, no effect.

negative-feedback.short: A loop in which the result of a signal turns the signal down, like a thermostat: insulin lowers blood glucose, and the lower glucose turns insulin release down.

peptide-hormone.short: A hormone made of a chain of amino acids (insulin, glucagon, growth hormone). It can't cross the cell membrane, so it acts on receptors on the cell surface, within seconds to minutes.

steroid-hormone.short: A hormone built from cholesterol (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone). It crosses the membrane, binds a receptor inside the cell and changes which genes are read, so its effects build over hours.

free-hormone.short: The part of a hormone in blood that is not bound to a carrier protein. For steroids such as testosterone and cortisol, the free part is thought to be the active part.

catecholamines.short: Adrenaline and noradrenaline (and dopamine): fast messengers made from the amino acid tyrosine, acting on α and β receptors on the cell surface.

adrenaline.short: Catecholamine released mainly by the adrenal medulla, the core of the adrenal glands. In exercise it speeds the heart, breaks down glycogen in muscle and liver and releases fat from fat tissue.

noradrenaline.short: Catecholamine released mainly by sympathetic nerve endings; the blood level is what spills over. It speeds the heart and narrows blood vessels in less active tissues.

beta-receptor.short: Surface receptor for adrenaline and noradrenaline. β₁ in the heart raises rate and force; β receptors in fat tissue drive lipolysis. Beta-blocker drugs block them.

glycogenolysis.short: Breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose units, by glycogen phosphorylase. In muscle it feeds glycolysis; in the liver it releases glucose into the blood.

lipolysis.short: Splitting stored triglyceride into fatty acids and glycerol. In fat tissue during exercise it is driven by catecholamines on β receptors and held back by insulin.

insulin.short: Peptide hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood glucose: it moves GLUT4 to the membrane and promotes storage of glycogen, fat and protein. It falls during sustained exercise.

glucagon.short: Peptide hormone from the pancreas that raises blood glucose: it drives glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis in the liver. It rises during sustained exercise.

cortisol.short: Steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex, the outer layer of the adrenal glands, released when the brain signals via the pituitary. It supports glucose supply by gluconeogenesis and by breaking down protein and fat.

growth-hormone.short: Peptide hormone from the pituitary, released in pulses (most in sleep and exercise). Among other roles it raises fat breakdown and helps spare glucose.

osmolality.short: How concentrated a fluid is in dissolved particles (mostly sodium in plasma). When plasma loses more water than salt, its osmolality rises and ADH is released.

vasopressin.short: Antidiuretic hormone: a peptide released from the back of the pituitary gland when plasma gets more concentrated (and by some other triggers). It makes the kidney keep water.

renin-angiotensin.short: Chain started by renin from the kidney: renin makes angiotensin I, which becomes angiotensin II; angiotensin II narrows vessels and releases aldosterone.

aldosterone.short: Steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex that makes the kidney keep sodium (and water with it) and lose potassium. Released mainly in response to angiotensin II.

plasma-volume.short: The volume of the fluid part of blood. It shrinks during hard exercise (concentrating everything in it) and expands with endurance training.

hyponatraemia.short: Low blood sodium during or after exercise, mainly from drinking more than the kidneys can excrete. Severe cases cause brain swelling and can kill.

testosterone.short: Steroid hormone made mainly in the testes (and in small amounts by the ovaries and adrenals), under the control of LH from the pituitary.

hpg-axis.short: Hypothalamus–pituitary–gonad axis: a signal from the hypothalamus (GnRH) makes the pituitary release LH and its partner FSH, which drive the testes or ovaries; their hormones feed back to damp the axis.

energy-availability.short: Energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure, per kg of fat-free mass per day: what is left for the rest of the body's work.

lh.short: Peptide hormone from the pituitary, released in pulses. In men it tells the testes to make testosterone; in women it drives ovulation and the ovaries' hormones.

reds.short: The International Olympic Committee's name for the health and performance problems caused by too little energy availability, in women and men. Earlier written RED-S.
